oneSentence: A token is one unit from a model’s vocabulary used to represent input or output, often smaller than a word.
plainExplanation:
People often imagine a language model processing one letter at a time or one whole word at a time. Usually, it does neither. A tokenizer first breaks text into units called tokens. A token might be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, a number, a space pattern or a special symbol.

When you type a prompt, the system converts its tokens into token IDs. A token ID is a number linked to one item in the model’s vocabulary, meaning the full set of tokens it can represent and choose from. The model processes the resulting sequence rather than relying on visible word boundaries.

When the model replies, it predicts output tokens in sequence. Software converts them back into readable text and may display the text gradually, piece by piece.

Token is often confused with tokenisation. A token is one unit after splitting. Tokenisation is the process that does the splitting. It is also often confused with a word, but tokens and words do not line up neatly across languages, writing systems, or even within one sentence.

Token counts matter because they affect cost, speed and limits. Many systems charge by token and set token limits for the context and output in one run.

everydayAnalogy.title: Sorting application forms into standard pieces
everydayAnalogy.story: An admissions office receives application forms from schools in Nairobi, Lima, Dhaka and Belgrade. Before staff can check them quickly, one worker cuts each form into standard pieces such as surname, given name, date, postcode and signature box. Some pieces match a whole field, while others split awkwardly because different schools format forms differently. The office system then processes those standard pieces one by one instead of looking at each page as a whole. Later, the pieces are arranged back into a readable application record.

mapping.analogyElement: standard pieces cut from each form
the worker dividing forms into pieces

mapping.aiElement: the model handling a sequence of token IDs
turning output tokens back into text

everydayAnalogy.limitation: Real tokenisation does not understand form fields the way office staff do. It usually splits by patterns learned for efficient processing, so the pieces may look odd to people and do not carry meaning as neatly as application sections.

visual.title: How one line of text becomes tokens
visual.learningObjective: Show that a model processes text as tokens, not as whole visible words, and that one sentence can split differently depending on the tokeniser.
visual.description: An interactive tokenizer lets the reader type or paste text and watch it split into coloured token blocks with counts and IDs. It shows that tokens can be words, word parts, punctuation or spaces, and that token totals affect limits and cost.

steps.label: Enter text
steps.explanation: The reader types a short sentence such as "Re-check Annex 3, please."
steps.visualInstruction: Place a text input at the top with sample text prefilled and a clear button beside it.

steps.label: Split into tokens
steps.explanation: The sentence appears below as adjacent coloured blocks. Each block shows one token boundary.
steps.visualInstruction: Render each token as a rounded rectangle in sequence, with thin gaps only where the tokeniser creates a new token.

steps.label: Inspect one token
steps.explanation: Selecting a block reveals its text piece, token ID and position in the sequence.
steps.visualInstruction: On click or keyboard focus, open a side panel with fields for token text, numeric ID and index number.

steps.label: Compare totals
steps.explanation: A counter updates to show how many tokens the input uses, reminding the reader that visible length and token count are not the same.
steps.visualInstruction: Display live counters for characters, words and tokens, with tokens visually emphasised.

visual.interaction: Readers can type their own text, paste examples in different languages, select token blocks to inspect IDs, and compare character, word and token counts as the display updates.
visual.accessibilityDescription: Screen-reader version: You enter text in an edit field. The page then reports the text split into an ordered list of tokens. For each token, it announces the token number, the exact text piece, and its token ID. It also reads summary counts for characters, words and tokens, followed by a short note that tokens may be whole words, parts of words, punctuation or spaces, so token count may differ from word count.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Reduced-motion version: token blocks appear instantly in a static row with no animated splitting or counting effects. Selecting a token updates the side panel without movement.

workedExample.scenario: Before sending the side-event concept note to the front office, the information management officer tests a heading instruction in the approved assistant.
workedExample.input: Draft a heading: Digital inclusion side event at 13:15.
process: The tokeniser divides the instruction into pieces from its vocabulary. An illustrative split might include "Draft", " a", " heading", ":", " Digital", " inclusion", " side", " event", " at", " 13", ":", "15" and "."
Each piece is represented by a token ID. These IDs, rather than the visible words themselves, are the sequence processed by the model.
The model predicts the next token ID, adds it to the sequence and repeats the process until the response is complete or an output limit is reached.
The software converts the generated token IDs back into readable text.
workedExample.result: The officer might receive: "Digital Inclusion Side Event, 13:15". The number of tokens will not necessarily match the number of words, and another model may split the same instruction differently because token vocabularies and tokenisers are model-specific.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At a duty station where the front office works in three languages, an information management officer is consolidating the language versions of a side-event concept note for circulation by close of business. The officer checks whether the approved assistant can take the drafting instruction and all three versions without losing the final paragraphs.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The context window is measured in tokens, not pages or words. Similar-length versions may use different numbers of tokens because each language is divided according to the model's vocabulary. The prompt, earlier exchanges and generated reply may all count towards the limit. Token counts can also affect output limits, response time and, where applicable, usage charges.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: A larger token allowance is not permission to include more sensitive material. Do not paste participant contact details, confidential delegation comments, tracked comments or other protected information into an external tool. Use only a tool approved for the material concerned, and include only what the drafting task requires.

whyItMatters: If you use or buy AI tools, token counts affect what fits, how fast replies arrive, and what the service may cost. Understanding tokens helps you set realistic expectations and compare systems more sensibly.
whereYouMayHearIt: In a vendor demo during a procurement meeting
At an ICT governance board review of context-window limits
During a technical handover on prompt and output limits
When an approved assistant cuts off a draft just before clearance

commonMisconceptions.misconception: One token always equals one word.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Many tokens are only part of a word, punctuation mark or space pattern. This is why short-looking text can still use several tokens.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Tokens are the same as letters or characters.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Characters are the visible symbols in writing. Tokens are processing units chosen by a tokenizer, so one token can contain several characters or only part of a visible word.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If two models see the same sentence, they must use the same tokens.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Different models can use different tokenizers and vocabularies, so the same text may split into different token sequences.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A token is a model input or output unit, such as a word piece, punctuation mark or special symbol.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: A token is a discrete symbol from a model-specific vocabulary, typically represented by a token ID after tokenisation; the model consumes and predicts sequences of these IDs during next-token generation.

keyTakeaway: Models process and generate sequences of tokens, which may be whole words, parts of words, punctuation marks or other vocabulary units.

quickCheck.question: Which statement about tokens is most accurate?
options: A token always matches one full word in every language.
A token is the same thing as tokenisation.
A token is one processing unit, which may be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation or spacing.
A token is another name for a model parameter.
quickCheck.explanation: A token is one unit the model handles. It does not always match a word, and it is different from tokenisation, which is the splitting process. It is also different from parameters, which are part of the model itself.

issues.problem: “Handles at one step” falsely suggests that input tokens are processed one by one. A language model can process an input sequence together, while next-token generation proceeds through successive prediction steps.
issues.fix: A token is one unit from a model’s vocabulary used to represent input or output, often smaller than a word.

issues.problem: The claim that producing one token at a time is why answers appear gradually confuses generation with interface behaviour. Software may stream generated text, but it may also buffer and display it later.
issues.fix: When the model replies, it predicts output tokens in sequence. Software converts them back into readable text and may display the text gradually, piece by piece.

issues.problem: The analogy says the office system processes pieces “one by one” and maps this to model processing. This repeats the false implication that a model must process input tokens sequentially.
issues.fix: Replace “The office system then processes those standard pieces one by one instead of looking at each page as a whole” with “The office system then processes the ordered pieces instead of looking at each page as a whole.” Change the mapping element to “the office system processing an ordered set of pieces”.

issues.problem: The learning objective promises to show that the same sentence can split differently under different tokenizers, but the interaction provides only one tokenizer and no comparison control. The visual therefore does not teach that part of the objective.
issues.fix: Let the reader choose two available tokenizers and show both token sequences and totals side by side. Update “Compare totals” to compare the two tokenizers as well as characters, words and tokens.

issues.problem: Calling every token a “piece of text” excludes special symbols that can also be vocabulary tokens. This also conflicts with the supplied definition of tokenisation.
issues.fix: A token is a model input or output unit, such as a word piece, punctuation mark or special symbol.

issues.problem: Option 2 merely equates the term with a process, and option 4 equates it with an unrelated internal setting. Together with the absolute wording in option 1, these distractors make option 3 obvious by form rather than requiring the learner to distinguish token, tokenisation and vocabulary. Option 3 is nevertheless the only defensible marked answer: option 1 is false because tokens need not be words, option 2 confuses a unit with the splitting process, and option 4 confuses a token with a learned setting.
issues.fix: Use these options: “The complete prompt is one token.”, “A token means the text-splitting process.”, “A token is one unit, such as a word, word part, punctuation or spacing.”, and “A token is the model’s full set of available units.” Keep correctOptionIndex as 2.

voicePass.note: Strengthened the workplace specificity, clarified that context can include both input and output, and made the tokenisation example explicitly illustrative rather than universal.
